formB.stem: During World War II, approximately 6 million women entered the American workforce in war industries that had previously excluded them. Even after the post-war reversal (when cultural pressure and policy encouraged women to return home, and returning veterans received job priority), the experience could not be entirely erased — it became part of the social memory that informed the feminist movement of the 1960s. formB.stem: During World War II, the Women's Army Corps (WAC), Navy WAVES, and other women's military branches allowed women to serve in non-combat military roles for the first time. This allowed women to contribute to the war effort without fully integrating the institution — a pattern of partial inclusion that acknowledged capability while limiting equality. The denial of equal veterans' benefits is particularly revealing: it maintained a status distinction that preserved the idea that women's service was qualitatively different (lesser) than men's. The dual messaging served a deliberate short-term strategy: heroic framing maximized wartime labor recruitment while the 'temporary' framing preserved the expectation that women would vacate industrial jobs when men returned, making the experiment appear non-threatening to the existing gender order.
